claims.claim: In 1935 the Forest Service established the 10 a.m. policy requiring every fire to be suppressed by 10 a.m. the day after its report.
claims.episode_span: In 1935 the agency formalized the “10 a.m. policy,” directing every district to have a fire under control by ten o’clock the morning after it was reported
claims.source_title: U.S. Forest Service Fire Suppression - Forest History Society
claims.supporting_quote: In 1935, the Forest Service established the so-called 10 a.m. policy, which decreed that every fire should be suppressed by 10 a.m. the day following its initial report.

claims.claim: The first advertising campaign featuring Smokey Bear began in 1944.
claims.episode_span: Smokey Bear, introduced in 1944 by the Forest Service and the Wartime Advertising Council
claims.supporting_quote: The first campaign featuring Smokey began in 1944; it used the slogan "Smokey Says – Care Will Prevent 9 out of 10 Forest Fires".

claims.claim: The 2000 Cerro Grande fire near Los Alamos began as a prescribed (controlled) burn that escaped control.
claims.episode_span: escaped prescribed burns such as the 2000 Cerro Grande fire near Los Alamos prompted stricter rules
claims.supporting_quote: The fire started as a controlled burn on May 4, 2000, and became uncontrolled owing to high winds and drought conditions.

claims.claim: Wildfire costs consumed 16 percent of the Forest Service budget in 1995 and more than 50 percent by 2015.
claims.episode_span: The Forest Service’s fire-suppression budget, roughly 16 percent of total agency spending in 1995, rose above 50 percent by 2020
claims.source_title: Firefighting burns up Forest Service budget - The Spokesman-Review
claims.supporting_quote: The U.S. Forest Service says it spent 16 percent of its budget fighting wildfires in 1995, that this year more than 50 percent of its budget will be spent on that purpose, and that, under current budget conditions, wildfire spending will constitute 67 percent or more of its budget by 2025.
